148.title: Halal earning
148.hook: halal is also how money is made: honest scales, no cheating, no interest (83:1–3; 2:275)
148.howItsDone: Muslims try to earn through honest work and trade, avoiding fraud, short measure and interest (riba); some use Islamic banking and home-finance products, and scholars differ on some modern cases.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the gray area, the shepherd at the edge of the pasture. Your line was leave what makes you doubt. Did you step back from one thing? Day one hundred forty-eight.

segments.voice: This week has mostly been about what goes into your mouth. The wide permitted middle. Good and wholesome. The name on the meat. The clear mind. The gray area. But the tradition doesn't stop at the plate. There's a question that comes before the food: how did you pay for it? In the tradition, a halal meal bought with money from cheating isn't really clean. Medina had a market, with scales and heaps of grain for sale. And the Prophet ﷺ walked through it. Today: halal earning.
screen: `A WEEK ABOUT THE PLATE.` → `HOW DID YOU PAY FOR IT?` → `THE MARKET IN MEDINA.`

segments.voice: Sahih Muslim tells the story. The Prophet ﷺ passed a heap of grain for sale, and put his hand into it. His fingers came out wet. The seller said the rain had gotten to it. The Prophet said: then why didn't you put the wet part on top, where people can see it? Whoever cheats is not of me. That's the heart of halal earning. The word is rizq, provision: everything that sustains you, from your salary to your lunch to the air. The Qur'an calls Allah ar-Razzaq, the Provider, and says there's no creature on earth whose provision isn't His concern. So in Islamic teaching rizq is given. But how you reach for it is yours. The Qur'an names some ways that aren't clean. Surah al-Mutaffifin begins: Woe unto the defrauders. It describes people who demand full measure when they buy, and give short measure when they sell. A thumb on the scale. And Surah al-Baqarah draws a line through finance: Allah permitteth trading and forbiddeth usury. The Arabic is riba, gain from lending money at interest. The majority view today applies that to ordinary bank interest, and Islamic banks offer accounts and home loans built another way; some scholars see modern interest differently. And the praise is just as clear. Bukhari reports that no one eats better food than what they earn with their own hands. Tirmidhi reports that the honest, trustworthy merchant will be with the prophets and the truthful. The biographies say the Prophet himself worked as a trader before his prophethood. Work isn't a lesser thing. Done honestly, some Muslims see it as a kind of worship.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one thing you earn or spend. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Bring to mind your work, or where your money comes from. Is there anywhere the wet grain is hidden underneath? A number rounded in your favor. A promise in an ad that isn't quite true. A charge you haven't looked at. Then think of one thing you'll spend money on this week. Where did it come from, and who was paid fairly on the way? Just look. If you pray, you can ask for clean provision. The bell holds the time.
Rizq. Provision: everything that sustains you, given by the Provider, reached for honestly. Today's word.
screen: `RIZQ — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: clean money. The next time you sell, bill, report or return something today, put the wet part on top where people can see it. Day one hundred forty-eight.

149.title: A smile is charity
149.hook: even meeting your brother with a cheerful face is charity (Tirmidhi)
149.howItsDone: Muslims give sadaqah, voluntary charity, in money and in kind, and count small acts, a smile, a kind word, directions, a helping hand, as sadaqah too.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: rizq, provision, reached for honestly. Your line was clean money. Did you put the wet part on top somewhere? Day one hundred forty-nine.
screen: `RIZQ — CLEAN MONEY.`

segments.voice: Charity usually sounds like money. A donation page. A jar by the register. A fundraiser with a thermometer drawing that never quite fills up. And if you don't have much money, it can feel like charity is for other people. Some poor companions said as much. Sahih Muslim reports they came to the Prophet ﷺ and complained: the wealthy are getting all the reward. They pray like us, they fast like us, and then they give from their extra money, and we can't. His answer widened the word. This week: charity as a habit. Today: a smile is charity.
screen: `CHARITY SOUNDS LIKE MONEY.` → `THE WEALTHY GET ALL THE REWARD.` → `HIS ANSWER WIDENED THE WORD.`

segments.voice: He told them: hasn't Allah given you things to give? Every glory to Allah is charity. Every praise is charity. Every Allahu akbar is charity. Telling someone about good is charity. The word is sadaqah. And its root is the surprising part: Lane's dictionary lists it under s-d-q, the root of sidq, truthfulness, and siddiq, the truthful. A hadith in Muslim calls sadaqah a proof, and commentators read it as faith showing it is true, faith with its hands out. In everyday use, zakat names the fixed yearly charity, which comes later this week, and sadaqah everything else: voluntary, any size, any time. And the hadith make everything else very wide. Bukhari reports: every good deed is sadaqah. Tirmidhi reports the Prophet ﷺ saying: your smile in the face of your brother is sadaqah. Pointing a lost person the right way is sadaqah. Pouring water from your bucket into someone else's is sadaqah. And Sahih Muslim adds: don't think little of any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face. So the poor companions had plenty to give after all. A face. A word. Directions. A little water. Sahih Muslim even says every joint in the body owes a charity each day the sun rises, and that helping a man lift his bags onto his mount pays one. The Qur'an protects the heart of it, too. Surah al-Baqarah says: A kind word with forgiveness is better than almsgiving followed by injury. A smile given freely can be worth more than a check handed over with a sneer. In these hadith, charity isn't a special occasion. It's a way of turning your face.
screen: `THE POOR COMPANIONS COMPLAIN.` · `SADAQAH — FROM THE ROOT OF TRUTH.` · `YOUR SMILE IN YOUR BROTHER'S FACE.` · `A KIND WORD, BETTER THAN ALMS WITH INJURY.` · then, large: `A FACE CAN GIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: smile at three people, starting in your mind. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Picture the first person you'll see after this: at home, on the street, at work. Picture meeting their eyes and letting your face soften, not a forced grin, just warmth. Now the second, someone you tend to ignore: a cashier, a driver, a cleaner. And the third, someone who's difficult for you. Notice where your face tightens, and let it ease. If you pray, you can intend each smile as sadaqah. The bell holds the time.
Sadaqah. Voluntary charity, from the root of truth: any good given freely, even a cheerful face. Today's word.
screen: `SADAQAH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a face can give. Smile at three real people today, on purpose, and count them on your fingers as you go. Day one hundred forty-nine.

150.title: Charity from the right hand
150.hook: give so the left hand doesn't know what the right gave (Bukhari)
150.howItsDone: Muslims are encouraged to give voluntary charity quietly, without mention, following the hadith of the seven shaded and 2:271, while some scholars allow zakat to be given openly to encourage others.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: sadaqah, charity from the root of truth, even a cheerful face. Your line was a face can give. Did you count three smiles? Day one hundred fifty.
screen: `SADAQAH — A FACE CAN GIVE.`

segments.voice: You've seen the photo. Someone hands a sandwich to a man sleeping on the street, and a friend films it from just the right angle. Or the charity gala where the donors' names go up on a screen, biggest first. Giving has a way of turning into a performance. There's a hadith that goes right at the wish to be seen, with a picture so odd it's hard to forget: a left hand that has no idea what the right hand just did. Today: charity from the right hand.
screen: `FILMED FROM THE RIGHT ANGLE.` → `NAMES ON A SCREEN, BIGGEST FIRST.` → `A LEFT HAND THAT DOESN'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: It's in Bukhari and Muslim: seven people whom Allah will shade on a day when there's no shade but His. A just ruler. A young person who grew up in worship. Someone whose heart is attached to the mosque. Two people who love each other for Allah's sake. A man called to sin by a woman of rank and beauty, who says, I fear Allah. Someone who remembered Allah alone, and whose eyes filled with tears. And the one for today: a person who gave charity and hid it, so that the left hand didn't know what the right hand gave. Your own other hand, inches away, doesn't find out. That's how quiet it's meant to be. No photo. No mention at dinner. Not even a proud glance at yourself. The Qur'an is gentle about it, not absolute. Surah al-Baqarah says that if you give openly, that is well, but if you hide it and give it to the poor, it is better for you. Open giving can encourage others, and some scholars say the yearly zakat may be given openly for that reason. But the commentators say the hidden gift protects two people: the one who receives, who keeps their dignity, and the one who gives, whose heart stays clean of showing off. The same surah warns against cancelling your charity with reminders and hurt. People tell a story, found in later collections, about Ali Zayn al-Abidin, a great-grandson of the Prophet ﷺ. For years, poor families in Medina found sacks of food at their doors at night, and never knew who brought them. When he died, they say, the deliveries stopped, and marks were found on his back from carrying them.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one secret gift. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Think of someone who could use something, anything: a coffee, a paid bill, a bag of groceries, a donation made in no one's name. Now plan it so no one finds out. Not them, not your friends, not your feed. Picture doing it. Now notice the little voice that wants someone to know. Don't fight it. Just let it be there, and don't obey it. If you pray, you can intend it for Allah alone. The bell holds the time.
Charity from the right hand. Giving so quietly that your own left hand doesn't know, one of the seven shaded on the last day. Today's word.

151.title: Zakat, plainly
151.hook: two and a half percent of savings held a year above a threshold, to the poor
151.carry: wealth has a share in it
151.howItsDone: Muslims whose savings stay above the nisab for a lunar year pay two and a half percent as zakat, often working it out once a year, and many choose Ramadan to pay it.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: charity from the right hand, so quiet the left hand doesn't know. Your line was hidden is best. Did you plan your secret gift? Day one hundred fifty-one.
screen: `CHARITY FROM THE RIGHT HAND — HIDDEN IS BEST.`

segments.voice: Sadaqah, the last two days, has been free: any size, any time, a smile, a secret gift. Now the path turns to the one that isn't. It's one of the five pillars, right next to the prayer and the fast. The Qur'an pairs it with prayer again and again: establish prayer, and pay the zakat. And unlike almost everything else in worship, it comes with a calculator. People sit at kitchen tables with bank statements and a price for gold, working out a number. It's surprisingly simple once someone lays it out. Today: zakat, plainly.
screen: `SADAQAH IS FREE. THIS ONE ISN'T.` → `PRAYER, AND ZAKAT.` → `WORSHIP WITH A CALCULATOR.`

segments.voice: Zakat comes from a root meaning two things at once: to purify, and to grow. In Surah at-Tawbah the Prophet ﷺ is told to take alms from people's wealth to purify them and make them grow. Giving some away is what keeps the rest clean. Here's how it works. First, a threshold: the nisab. Below it, you owe no zakat at all. The hadith set it in the coins of the time: two hundred silver dirhams, or twenty gold dinars. Today scholars usually convert that to about eighty-five grams of gold or about five hundred ninety-five grams of silver, and they differ on which to use. Silver gives a lower threshold, so more people pay and the poor receive more; gold gives a higher one. Second, a year. If your savings stay at or above the nisab for a full lunar year, zakat is due. Third, the rate: one fortieth, two and a half percent, of what you hold. Cash, savings, gold and silver, goods for trade. Not your home, your car, your clothes or your tools. Crops and livestock have their own rules. Two and a half percent. Not a punishing amount. But once a year, every year, it moves wealth from those who have it toward those who don't. The Qur'an describes the good in Surah adh-Dhariyat this way: And in their wealth the beggar and the outcast had due share. Due share. In this picture, the poor person's part was always in your account. Zakat isn't a gift from you. It's handing over what was already theirs.
screen: `ZAKAT — TO PURIFY AND TO GROW.` · `NISAB — THE THRESHOLD.` · `A FULL LUNAR YEAR.` · `ONE FORTIETH, TWO AND A HALF PERCENT.` · then, large: `THE BEGGAR HAD DUE SHARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to learn your own nisab figure. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Picture your savings, just roughly, without judging the number. Now picture a line: the nisab, the price of about eighty-five grams of gold or five hundred ninety-five of silver. Are you above it or below it? You don't need to know yet. After the bell, look up today's price and do the sum; many mosques and charities have simple calculators. For now, just sit with the idea that part of what you hold may already belong to someone else. The bell holds the time.
Nisab. The threshold of wealth, held for a year, above which zakat of two and a half percent is due. Today's word.
screen: `NISAB — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: wealth has a share in it. Look up today's nisab figure, and write it down somewhere you'll find it again. Day one hundred fifty-one.

152.title: The eight who receive
152.hook: the Qur'an names who zakat is for: the poor, the needy, debtors, travelers and others (9:60)
152.howItsDone: Muslims direct their zakat to the eight categories named in 9:60, often through mosques or zakat organizations, preferring local recipients, and not to their own parents or children.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: nisab, the threshold that has to be held for a year, and the two and a half percent due above it. Your line was wealth has a share in it. Did you look up the figure? Day one hundred fifty-two.
screen: `NISAB — WEALTH HAS A SHARE IN IT.`

segments.voice: So you've worked out the number. Two and a half percent, sitting in your account, ready to go. Now what? Do you hand it to the first person who asks? Drop it in any collection box? Give it to your cousin who's always broke? Most giving in life is left to the giver's judgment. But zakat is unusual. The Qur'an doesn't just say give. It gives you the list. One verse, in Surah at-Tawbah, names exactly who zakat is for. Eight kinds of people. Eight addresses. Today: the eight who receive.
screen: `THE NUMBER IS READY. NOW WHAT?` → `NOT JUST GIVE: HERE'S THE LIST.` → `EIGHT ADDRESSES.`

segments.voice: Chapter nine, verse sixty. In Pickthall's translation it begins: The alms are only for the poor and the needy. Then it goes on. Here are all eight. One, the poor, al-fuqara'. Two, the needy, al-masakin. Scholars differ on which of those two is worse off, but together they're the people who can't cover the basics. Three, those who collect and manage zakat: the workers, paid from it so the system runs. Four, those whose hearts are to be reconciled: people new to Islam, or whose goodwill the community needs. Five, to free the captives. In the Prophet's time that meant helping enslaved people buy their freedom; some scholars today apply it to freeing people from captivity and trafficking. Six, the debtors, people crushed by debts they took on for a decent reason. Seven, in the cause of Allah. Classically this meant those fighting in defense of the community; some modern scholars read it more widely, for example for education and dawah, and others keep it narrow. And eight, the wayfarer, the traveler stranded far from home, even if they're rich back there. The verse ends: a duty from Allah. Notice what the list doesn't name: the mosque's new carpet, or the giver's own family. The jurists say zakat isn't paid to your own parents or children, because you already owe them support. Bukhari reports that when the Prophet ﷺ sent Mu'adh to Yemen, he told him to take it from their rich and return it to their poor. Local, specific, human. Zakat doesn't vanish into a fog called charity. It has addresses.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn the eight categories, with faces. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Count them on your fingers, slowly, and for each, picture a real person. The poor. The needy. The one who collects. A heart being welcomed. A captive. Someone drowning in debt. The cause of Allah. A traveler stranded at a station at midnight. Eight fingers, eight faces. Go through them twice. By the second time, you'll have the list. Notice which face stays with you longest. The bell holds the time.
The eight who receive. The people Surah at-Tawbah names for zakat: the poor, the needy, the workers, reconciled hearts, captives, debtors, the cause of Allah, and the traveler. Today's word.

153.title: Charity that keeps flowing
153.hook: a well, a tree, knowledge taught: good that runs after you're gone (Muslim)
153.howItsDone: Muslims give sadaqah jariyah by funding wells, planting trees, endowing schools and mosques, and teaching, and often make it on behalf of parents who have died.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eight who receive, named in Surah at-Tawbah. Your line was it has addresses. Did you find one real place near you? Day one hundred fifty-three.
screen: `THE EIGHT WHO RECEIVE — IT HAS ADDRESSES.`

segments.voice: A park bench with a small brass plate on it: in memory of someone nobody sitting there has met. A tree someone's grandfather planted, still giving shade to people who don't know his name. A teacher long gone, whose way of explaining fractions is still being passed from one kid to the next. Most of what we do is gone by evening. A few things keep running long after we've stopped. The hadith has a name for those things, and it's a picture of water. Today: charity that keeps flowing.
screen: `A BENCH WITH A BRASS PLATE.` → `SHADE FROM A GRANDFATHER'S TREE.` → `A FEW THINGS KEEP RUNNING.`

segments.voice: Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet ﷺ saying: when a person dies, their deeds come to an end, except for three. A charity that keeps flowing. Knowledge that people keep benefiting from. And a righteous child who prays for them. The first is sadaqah jariyah. Jariyah means running, flowing, like a stream. It's the charity that keeps paying out after the giver has gone. One example is a real well. The reports say that in Medina there was a well called Rumah whose owner sold its water, and the Muslims were short of it. The Prophet asked who would buy the well and make it free for everyone. The companion Uthman bought it, the reports in Tirmidhi say, and gave it away. People say that well still gives water today. Trees are the second picture. Bukhari and Muslim report that whenever a Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop, and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, it's charity for them. Every bite, for as long as it grows. And in another report, the Prophet said: if the Hour comes and one of you has a sapling in his hand, let him plant it. Even at the end of the world, plant. Across the centuries, Muslims turned this into institutions: endowments called waqf that paid for hospitals, schools, public fountains and travelers' inns, some still running long after their founders died. But it doesn't need to be big. Teaching a child to read is flowing knowledge. A recipe you pass on. A tree in a yard. Something you start, that keeps going without you.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plant or teach something, starting here. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Think of one thing you know how to do well: cook a dish, fix a bike, recite a short surah, write a letter, calm a crying baby. Now think of one person who'd be helped by learning it. Picture teaching them. Or picture a seed going into soil, in a pot, a yard, a community garden, and the shade it might give when you're not there. Choose one, plant or teach, and decide when. If you pray, you can intend it as sadaqah jariyah. The bell holds the time.
Sadaqah jariyah. Flowing charity: a well, a tree, knowledge taught, good that keeps running after you're gone. Today's word.
screen: `SADAQAH JARIYAH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the well keeps giving. Teach one person one useful thing today, or put one seed in soil, and let it run without you. Day one hundred fifty-three.

154.title: The neighbor
154.hook: Jibril kept urging kindness to the neighbor until the Prophet ﷺ thought neighbors would inherit (Bukhari)
154.tomorrow: Removing a stone from the road
154.howItsDone: Muslims give special weight to neighbors, of any faith: sharing food, visiting, helping and avoiding any harm to them, following the hadith of Jibril and the neighbor.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: sadaqah jariyah, the well, the tree and the knowledge that keep running. Your line was the well keeps giving. Did you teach or plant something? Day one hundred fifty-four.
screen: `SADAQAH JARIYAH — THE WELL KEEPS GIVING.`

segments.voice: Quick question: what's the name of the person who lives closest to you? Not the closest friend. The closest person. The one on the other side of your wall, or across the hall, or next door. A lot of us don't know. We know people on the other side of the world by their usernames, and we nod at the person ten feet away without ever learning their name. We send money to causes overseas, which is good, and have never knocked on the door beside ours. In Islam, charity has a starting point, and it's on the other side of your wall. Today: the neighbor.
screen: `WHO LIVES CLOSEST TO YOU?` → `A NOD, TEN FEET AWAY.` → `CHARITY HAS A STARTING POINT.`

segments.voice: Bukhari and Muslim report the Prophet ﷺ saying: Jibril kept urging me to be good to the neighbor, so much that I thought he would make the neighbor an heir. An heir. Someone with a legal share in what you leave behind, like family. That's how often the angel came back to it. The Qur'an names neighbors in Surah an-Nisa, in a list of those to be good to: parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbor who is related to you and the neighbor who is a stranger, the companion at your side. And Bukhari reports a warning so strong the Prophet said it three times: by Allah, he does not believe. Who? The one whose neighbor is not safe from his harm. The hadith get very practical. Sahih Muslim reports him telling the companion Abu Dharr: when you make a stew, add some extra water, and look to your neighbors. Stretch the pot. Bukhari reports him telling women not to think any gift to a neighbor too small, even a sheep's hoof. And a neighbor isn't defined by faith. Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud report that the companion Abdullah ibn Amr had a sheep slaughtered, and when he came home the first thing he asked was: have you given some to our Jewish neighbor? Because he had heard the Prophet's words about Jibril and the neighbor. Scholars have argued over how far a neighborhood stretches. But the principle is simpler than any measuring. Before the world, the house next door. Before the cause, the name.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan to take something to a neighbor. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Picture the doors nearest yours, one by one. Which neighbors do you know? Which don't you? Pick one. Now picture something small you could bring them: extra from dinner, a few pieces of fruit, a note with your name and number, even just a hello. Not too small, remember: even a sheep's hoof. Picture knocking. Picture their face. If it makes you nervous, notice that, and breathe through it. The bell holds the time.
The neighbor. The one next door, whose rights Jibril urged so often the Prophet thought they would inherit. Today's word.
screen: `THE NEIGHBOR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: start next door. Knock on one neighbor's door this week with something small in your hand, and if you don't know their name, learn it. Day one hundred fifty-four.
